newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal confident of EMU berth despite doubters.
newsitem.headline: Portugal confident of EMU berth despite doubters.

text.p: Portugal is convinced that it can be amongst a European elite to launch the single currency in 1999 whatever the doubts of international markets.

According to a Reuter poll of 45 economists from across Europe published on Thursday, Portugal has only a 24 percent chance of being chosen when European Union leaders meet in the spring of next year to decide who can join monetary union.
But the view from Lisbon is altogether more optimistic.
"I would rate the chances of Portugal being in the single currency in 1999 as 70 percent," said Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa, leader of the main opposition party, the Social Democrats.

The conservative leader, whose party recently joined the Socialist government to table a joint motion in parliament backing Portugal's campaign for single currency membership, said that he was confident that the country would meet the economic requirements for entry.
"I am 90 percent sure," he told journalists on Thursday.

Socialist government ministers, who have made qualifying for the single currency their top policy priority, have never been less than convinced. "I have absolutely no doubt we will be in (monetary union)," deputy finance minister Fernando Teixeira dos Santos told Reuters in a recent interview.
International economists who follow Portugal closely say that the country has a good chance of passing key economic tests, with the budget deficit and inflation both set to be below entry limits.
Portugal's cause was helped by a ruling last week by the European Union's statistics body Eurostat that would result in both lower debt and inflation levels than officially calculated.
"Just looking at the figures, it would appear that they could be there," said economist Deborah Bennellick of UBS Ltd in London.
Portugal has budgeted for a state deficit of 2.9 percent in 1997, inside the three percent ceiling.
Although inflation edged up over the turn of the year, it is widely expected to resume its downward path from the spring to hit the government's 2.5 percent target by the year's end.

But even many economists who are optimistic on the numbers prefer to be cautious when it comes to forecasting whether Portugal and its Iberian neighbour Spain will be in the vanguard of economic and monetary union (EMU).
Rebelo da Sousa said that the risk of some sort of political interference explained why he was more certain of Portugal meeting the requirements than of its gaining entry.
Economists say that the suspicion is that international political considerations will take a hand, particularly if, as many expect, founder EU member Italy fails to pass muster.
"If Italy does not make it, it would be politically difficult to let Spain in. And the argument goes for Portugal as well," said another London analyst.
It is a view that the Portuguese, who resent attempts to lump southern European countries together in a so-called 'Club Med', have been seeking to combat.

On recent visits to European Union partners France and Luxembourg, both expected to form part of an EMU core, Prime Minister Antonio Guterres won pledges that the decision on single currency membership would be based on economics and not politics.
"We received express guarantees that whoever meets the targets should be allowed in," a government spokesman said.
